newsitem.title: Italy: FOCUS-Olivetti meeting called, shares leap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti meeting called, shares leap.

text.p: Italy's Olivetti group called a board meeting on Wednesday which could signal a new upheaval in its top management after the company side-stepped key questions about its business put by market regulators.
Olivetti shares, which began trading two hours after the rest of the Italian market opened, rebounded from record lows and triggered an automatic suspension after hiting a 10 percent trading limit.
Olivetti said in a statement it had called the board meeting for 1600 GMT but gave no details of what was on the agenda.
Financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said chief executive Francesco Caio was likely either to resign or to be ousted only three months after taking up the post.
Olivetti's former chairman Carlo De Benedetti, still the biggest shareholder in the company, was reported by Il Sole to be the prime mover behind a plan to eject Caio.
De Benedetti was himself forced off the board only 15 days ago after a showdown with Caio, his former assistant, but is now widely reported to be thirsting for revenge.

The meeting follows hot on the heels of a lengthy statement issued earlier in the day in which Olivetti gave details of its affairs in response to a demand by stock market regulator Consob for answers to 16 key questions on its finances.

Olivetti's reply left equity analysts none the wiser as to the true financial state of the loss-making company. Olivetti said it could not divulge confidential information about talks under way on future divestments or strategic accords.

It also said it could not state its consolidated financial situation for the end of August 1996 until the first week of October. It set a value on its stock of computer hardware without detailing -- as the market had wanted -- whether the equipment was outdated and unsellable or state-of-the-art.
In the marketplace, authorities delayed the start of trading in Olivetti shares for two hours to allow the market time to assess the information supplied by the group.
The share swiftly rose to 511 lire per share tripping the 10 percent fluctuation limit on unusually high turnover of 33 million shares. Trade was due to resume at 1200 GMT.
on Tuesday the stock had repeatedly triggered suspension by falling to the floor of its trading limits and forging a new record low of 465 lire.

Brokers were sceptical about the buying interest. "There's nothing particularly new in the 16 answers. People are watching and keeping their distance. We haven't really got much more information than we had yesterday evening," one said.

Olivetti, one of Italy's entrepreneurial success stories of the 1980s, has been caught in a snowballing crisis involving doubts about the accuracy of its first-half accounts since the De Benedetti's shock resignation on September 3.

Caio, 39, new chairman Antonio Tesone and De Benedetti himself are being investigated by magistrates in Olivetti's home town of Ivrea who suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its affairs, judicial sources say.

That inquiry and Consob's questions were all prompted by the resignation of Olivetti director general Renzo Francesconi the day after De Benedetti sood down. Francesconi said he disagreed with figures in the half-year results.
After questioning Caio and Francesconi, Consob then told Olivetti it wanted more data which must also be released to the market.
Olivetti's financial exposure has spiralled since the group completed a massive 2.26 trillion lire ($1.48 billion) rights issue at the end of last year.
The company said its net debt at the end of June totalled 1.26 trillion but analysts say that interest charges paid by the company suggest that it may really owe far more.
